scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: Armed struggle is a legitimate and necessary means of establishing religious rule.
Political change through preaching and elections alone is too slow to correct a society that has strayed this far.
A vanguard willing to use force is sometimes required to bring about a truly religious order.
Waiting on gradual persuasion cedes the field to those actively working against religious values.
Jihad or holy struggle, in its militant sense, remains a legitimate instrument of religious politics today.
Revolutionary upheaval, not incremental reform, is what real religious renewal requires.
Religious renewal should be pursued through preaching, education, and participation in existing political processes.
Elections and gradual religious education are a legitimate and sufficient path to a more religious society.
Armed struggle against the existing order tends to discredit religious politics rather than advance it.
Patient civic and missionary work builds more lasting change than confrontation does.
Working within the existing political system is compatible with a serious commitment to religious values.
A movement that renounces violence can still achieve real religious influence over society.
Trained religious scholars should hold formal authority to govern or to veto un-Islamic or ungodly legislation.
The guardianship of the jurist, or an equivalent clerical office, is a legitimate model of government.
Ordinary political leaders should be answerable to religious scholars on matters of law and policy.
A council of clergy should have the final word when law conflicts with religious teaching.
Formal clerical office is a more reliable guardian of religious law than lay politicians.
The scholars of the faith, not elected politicians, should have ultimate authority over what counts as legitimate law.
Governance should remain in the hands of lay political leaders, with clergy limited to moral and religious guidance.
Formal clerical rule over the state risks corrupting the clergy as much as it risks corrupting the state.
A lay government that consults religious scholars, without being bound by them, is the better model.
Political authority and religious authority should be held by different people, even in a religious state.
Clergy who govern directly tend to lose the moral authority that comes from staying above politics.
The state should implement religious law through its own institutions, not cede governing power to the clergy.
Centuries of legal scholarship and interpretive tradition remain the proper guide to applying scripture today.
Sound religious law depends on trained jurisprudence, not on reading scripture without that tradition.
Interpretive schools built up over generations should not be casually discarded in favour of individual readings.
A jurist's ruling, grounded in the accumulated tradition, carries real authority in applying the text.
Scripture has to be read through the accumulated wisdom of scholars across generations, not in isolation.
Bypassing centuries of legal tradition in favour of a direct reading of scripture invites serious error.
Believers should return directly to the original scripture, setting aside centuries of accumulated interpretation.
Much of the later interpretive tradition represents a departure from, not a clarification of, the original texts.
The earliest generation's practice, not later scholarly elaboration, is the authoritative guide.
Later schools of interpretation added innovations that a return to the source text should strip away.
A direct, literal reading of scripture is more reliable than layers of scholarly commentary.
Purifying religious practice means stripping away accumulated interpretation and returning to the original sources.
The community of the faithful transcends nationality and is the proper political community.
Believers everywhere belong to a single community that should take priority over national citizenship.
National borders are a secondary, even artificial, division within the true community of the faith.
A religious polity should aim to unite believers across national lines, not confine itself to one nation.
Loyalty to the faith community should outweigh loyalty to any particular nation-state.
The ultimate political horizon is the community of believers, not any single national state.
The religious state should be organised around and for a particular nation and its people.
Religious and national identity are properly fused, not separated into rival loyalties.
A religious state has legitimate obligations to its own nation that come before universal religious solidarity.
The nation, not the wider community of believers, is the primary vessel of religious political life today.
Religious politics should serve the particular people and homeland it arises from, not a universal community.
A specific national mission is central to this movement's religious project, not incidental to it.
The wealthy have a binding religious obligation to redistribute a real share of their wealth to the poor.
Charging interest and similar exploitative financial practices should be prohibited by religious law.
Economic policy should actively narrow the gap between rich and poor as a matter of religious duty.
A religious economy should place limits on private accumulation in the name of communal welfare.
Religious welfare obligations should be enforced through the state, not left to voluntary charity alone.
Concentrated private wealth is a religious as well as a social problem that policy should address.
A religious state should welcome commerce and free exchange rather than impose heavy redistributive obligations.
Private property and market exchange are fully compatible with, and even blessed by, religious teaching.
Merchants and entrepreneurs deserve religious and social respect, not suspicion, for their success.
Religious law protects private property and trade at least as much as it demands redistribution.
A prosperous merchant class strengthens a religious society rather than threatening it.
Voluntary charity, not state-enforced redistribution, is the proper religious response to poverty.
The modern nation-state, its constitutions, and its bureaucracy should be actively captured and used to enact religious law.
A movement can and should work through existing state institutions to establish religious governance.
Modern administrative capacity, once captured, is a legitimate and useful tool for religious governance.
There's nothing wrong in principle with running for office and legislating within a modern constitutional state.
Using the machinery of a modern state is compatible with, and even necessary for, implementing religious law at scale.
A religious movement should be pragmatic about using whatever modern institutions are available to it.
The modern nation-state and its man-made constitutions are themselves illegitimate and should be rejected, not captured.
Sovereignty belongs to God alone, which makes man-made constitutions a rival and false claim to authority.
A truly religious order requires dismantling the modern state, not winning elections within it.
Legitimate religious governance can't be built by working through institutions premised on human, not divine, sovereignty.
Modern constitutionalism is itself part of the problem a religious movement exists to overturn.
Participating in the modern state's institutions concedes their legitimacy in a way true believers shouldn't accept.
The community of the truly faithful should be broad, including those who differ on secondary matters of practice or doctrine.
Fellow believers should not be readily declared apostates over disagreements in interpretation.
Unity among believers of different schools and traditions matters more than doctrinal precision on every point.
Excommunicating other believers over doctrinal disputes weakens the community more than it purifies it.
A wide, tolerant view of who counts as a genuine believer serves the community better than a narrow one.
Doctrinal disagreement among believers should be a matter for debate, not grounds for exclusion.
Believers who deviate seriously from correct doctrine or practice should be considered outside the true faith.
Maintaining doctrinal purity sometimes requires declaring even nominal believers apostate.
A community that tolerates significant doctrinal deviation has compromised the faith itself.
Firm boundaries around correct belief and practice are necessary, even when they exclude many who call themselves believers.
Doctrinal laxity is a greater danger to the faith than the divisiveness of strict boundaries.
True religious renewal requires clearly separating the genuinely faithful from those who only appear to be.
Western political and cultural influence is a corrupting force that religious politics should actively resist.
Accommodation with Western powers tends to compromise a movement's religious integrity.
The West's global dominance is itself a target that religious politics is right to confront.
Cooperation with Western governments should be treated with deep suspicion, if not rejected outright.
Resisting Western cultural and political influence is as central to this movement as its domestic religious goals.
A movement that grows too close to Western powers has already begun to lose its religious purpose.
Practical cooperation and diplomacy with Western powers can serve a religious movement's interests without betraying them.
Religious politics doesn't require treating the West as a fundamental enemy.
A pragmatic relationship with Western governments is compatible with maintaining religious conviction.
Isolating a movement from all relations with Western powers weakens it more than it protects it.
Confrontation with the West should not be an end in itself for a religious movement.
A religious movement can pursue its domestic goals without making opposition to the West central to its identity.
